body:
Childhood & Early Life

Thomas Chatterton was born on 20 November 1752 in Bristol, in a house beside the great medieval church of St Mary Redcliffe. His father, a schoolmaster and sexton of the church, died three months before he was born. His mother, Sarah, raised him and his sister Mary on what she earned from sewing and teaching girls.

He was slow to speak and thought to be dull, until at about six he fell in love with the illuminated capitals of an old music book and learned to read from it. After that he never stopped. He read in the attic, in the churchyard and in the muniment room above the north porch of Redcliffe, where his uncle's family kept chests of old parchment. Those parchments became the raw material for his greatest invention.

What They Did & Why They're Remembered

At about twelve he began producing poems he said were by Thomas Rowley, a fifteenth-century priest of Bristol. He wrote them in a faked archaic spelling, on parchment he rubbed with ochre and soot to age it. There was no Rowley. Chatterton had invented the man, his patron William Canynge, and a whole lost medieval Bristol to put them in.

The forgeries fooled many people for years. He is remembered because the poems were good, and because he was dead at seventeen. The Romantics made him their patron saint of the neglected young genius. Keats dedicated Endymion to his memory, Wordsworth called him "the marvellous boy," and Shelley and Coleridge both wrote about him.

Family Life

Chatterton supported his mother and sister in his own way, by sending them small gifts from London and promising that fortune was on its way. His letters home are cheerful and boastful, full of imagined patrons and money about to arrive. His mother kept them. After his death she learned how hungry he had been when he wrote them.

Romantic Life

No great love is recorded for him. He had a few flirtations with Bristol girls, and he wrote verses to a "Miss Hoyland" and others. His heart seems to have gone into the lost-lover figures in his poems. The most famous of them is the girl who sings over her dead love in the song below.

Life Until Death

At sixteen he was apprenticed to a Bristol attorney, a job he hated, and he wrote his Rowley poems at his desk. In April 1770 he went to London to live by his pen. He wrote political letters, satires, songs and essays for the magazines, and was paid very little for any of it. The great men he had hoped to impress, including Horace Walpole, who had rejected the Rowley poems after learning they were forged, did nothing for him.

By August he was starving. He was too proud to take food from his landlady, a plasterer's wife named Mrs Angell. On the night of 24 August 1770 he took arsenic in his attic room at Brooke Street, Holborn, and tore up his papers. He was seventeen. He was buried in a pauper's ground, and the exact spot was never recorded.

His death became a symbol. Henry Wallis painted a famous picture of him lying on the attic bed in 1856.

Their Works

Here is the song everyone remembers, sung by Birtha in his Rowley play Ælla. It is written in his invented medieval spelling, and the refrain is the heart of it.

The Minstrel's Song, from Ælla

Here is a short piece of his own voice, written in his own name at sixteen. It is a fragment of a poem he titled "Sentiment" in 1769.

Sentiment (1769, opening)

Since we can die but once, what matters it,
If rope or garter, poison, pistol, sword,
Slow-wasting sickness or the sudden burst
Of valve arterial in the noble parts,
Curtail the miseries of human life?
Tho' varied is the Cause, the Effect's the same;
All to one common Dissolution tends.

The first poem is mourning for a death. The second is a seventeen-year-old calmly arguing about his own. Together they are a good picture of Chatterton.
epi: The marvellous boy who invented a medieval poet
quote: Mie love ys dedde, Gon to hys death-bedde, Al under the wyllowe tree.
